items.answer: For: Oil prices quadrupled in 1973-74 and rose again in 1979. Energy costs raised prices across the economy. Each shock was followed by recession. items.stem: Priya is planning an answer to the question: “‘The oil crises were the main cause of stagflation in the 1970s.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Priya could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: the oil shocks made stagflation severe, but its roots lay in the spending of the 1960s and declining competitiveness. Support: Oil prices quadrupled in 1973-74 and rose again in 1979. Energy costs raised prices across the economy. Challenge: Inflation was already rising in the late 1960s because of Vietnam spending. Productivity growth slowed and foreign competition increased.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: A revision guide lists these reasons why the US economy suffered stagflation in the 1970s. A: Falling productivity growth. B: Oil price shocks in 1973 and 1979 raised costs. C: The collapse of Bretton Woods weakened the dollar. Explain which of these was the most important reason.
items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: Falling productivity growth. B: Oil price shocks in 1973 and 1979 raised costs. C: The collapse of Bretton Woods weakened the dollar. Possible judgement: the oil shocks were the trigger, but inflation had deep roots in the spending of the 1960s and US competitiveness was declining.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: Study Sources C and D. Source C: a newspaper report from a petrol station, 1974 (illustrative). “The queue stretched for half a mile. Drivers who had waited two hours were told the pumps were dry. Prices have doubled since the autumn.” Source D: Jimmy Carter, televised address, July 1979 (summary). Carter spoke of a "crisis of confidence" among Americans and called on them to save energy and work together to overcome the nation's problems. Identify one similarity and one difference between Sources C and D on the US economy in the 1970s.
items.answer: Source C: It shows shortages and rising prices caused by the oil crisis. Source D: It shows the president presenting the crisis as one of national morale. A similarity and a difference must each be supported by details from both sources.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a similarity and 1 for supporting it from both sources; 1 mark for a difference and 1 for supporting it from both sources [4]

items.stem: A student writes: “Reagan balanced the federal budget.” Is this accurate? Explain your answer using your own knowledge.
items.answer: Not accurate. Deficits grew and the debt roughly tripled.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a correct judgement; 1 mark for accurate supporting knowledge [2]

items.stem: A revision guide lists these reasons why the US economy recovered after 1982. A: Oil prices fell in the mid-1980s. B: Tax cuts boosted spending and investment. C: Inflation fell after Volcker's tight money policy. Explain how these reasons were linked and decide which mattered most.
items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: Oil prices fell in the mid-1980s. B: Tax cuts boosted spending and investment. C: Inflation fell after Volcker's tight money policy. Possible judgement: falling inflation and oil prices, together with a large fiscal stimulus, explain the recovery more than supply-side theory.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: ‘Reaganomics revived the US economy.’ Discuss.
items.answer: For: Inflation fell and growth was strong from 1983. Millions of new jobs were created. Tax cuts and deregulation encouraged enterprise. Against: Volcker's monetary policy, not Reagan's, defeated inflation. Deficits and debt soared. Manufacturing decline and inequality grew. Judgement: the economy revived in the 1980s, but its recovery owed as much to falling inflation and deficit spending as to supply-side policies.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): a focused, balanced and analytical answer with a sustained, well-supported judgement; precise and relevant knowledge throughout. Level 4 (13-16): analysis of both sides with a judgement, though not fully sustained or supported. Level 3 (9-12): some analysis, but one-sided or uneven, or with descriptive passages. Level 2 (5-8): mainly descriptive or narrative, with limited links to the question. Level 1 (1-4): general, unsupported or irrelevant points. (The examination essay is marked out of 30; levels are scaled.) Agree / supporting: Inflation fell and growth was strong from 1983. Millions of new jobs were created. Tax cuts and deregulation encouraged enterprise. Disagree / other factors: Volcker's monetary policy, not Reagan's, defeated inflation. Deficits and debt soared. Manufacturing decline and inequality grew. Possible judgement: the economy revived in the 1980s, but its recovery owed as much to falling inflation and deficit spending as to supply-side policies. [20]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this description: “the movement of people, especially white middle-class families, from cities to new suburbs”.
items.answer: Suburbanisation
items.markingKey: Suburbanisation: the movement of people, especially white middle-class families, from cities to new suburbs. [1]

items.stem: Which of these statements is accurate?
options: Eisenhower called for higher defence spending in his farewell address.
Car ownership and television spread rapidly in the 1950s.
Inflation was below 3 per cent throughout the 1970s.
items.answer: Car ownership and television spread rapidly in the 1950s.
items.markingKey: By 1960 most households had a television. The other statements are inaccurate. [1]

items.stem: Lucas is planning an answer to the question: “How far was government policy responsible for the post-war boom?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Lucas could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: government policy supported and shaped the boom, but its main driver was private consumer demand in an economy without serious competitors. Support: The GI Bill and federal mortgage support. Defence spending. Challenge: Private consumer demand and savings. US industrial dominance with weak foreign competitors.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: Read the sources carefully. Source A: Michael Harrington, The Other America, 1962 (summary). Harrington argued that around 40 to 50 million Americans lived in poverty, hidden from the affluent in rural areas and city slums. Source B: an advertisement for a suburban housing development, 1950s (description). The advertisement shows a smiling white family outside a new house with a car in the drive, under the slogan "Your own home - no money down for veterans". “All Americans shared in the prosperity of the post-war boom.” How far do Sources A and B support this view?
items.answer: Source A challenges: it shows many Americans excluded from prosperity. Evaluation: Harrington was a socialist campaigner and his estimates were debated. Source B supports: it presents prosperity as widely shared. Evaluation: it is advertising and shows only the image the builder wanted. Grouping: support B; challenge A. A judgement must weigh how convincing each group is, using provenance and own knowledge, rather than counting sources.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): evaluates the sources (provenance, purpose, context, cross-reference) to show how far they support AND challenge the view, reaching a supported judgement. Level 4 (13-16): uses the sources to support AND challenge the view and evaluates some of them. Level 3 (9-12): uses the sources at face value to support AND challenge. Level 2 (5-8): uses the sources to support OR challenge. Level 1 (1-4): writes about the topic without valid use of the sources. (The examination version uses four sources and 25 marks; levels are scaled.) [20]

items.stem: What is meant by “military-industrial complex”?
options: Galbraith's 1958 book arguing that private wealth coexisted with public poverty.
Reagan's economic policies of tax cuts, deregulation, reduced domestic spending and tight money.
The post-war system of fixed exchange rates tied to the dollar, which collapsed in 1971-73.
Eisenhower's term for the alliance of the armed forces and arms industries.
items.answer: Eisenhower's term for the alliance of the armed forces and arms industries.
items.markingKey: Military-industrial complex: Eisenhower's term for the alliance of the armed forces and arms industries. [1]

items.stem: Sipho ends an essay on “How far did the Cold War shape the US economy, 1945-68?” with this conclusion: “The Cold War economy was a major support for growth and shaped its regional pattern, but consumer demand was the main engine.” Explain one piece of evidence that supports this conclusion and one point a critic could make against it.
items.answer: Evidence the conclusion rests on (either strand of the judgement), for example: Defence spending stimulated industry and technology. / Consumer demand was the main engine of growth. Possible criticism: the conclusion may underplay the point that Aerospace and electronics grew in the Sunbelt.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for relevant supporting evidence and 1 mark for explaining how it supports the judgement; 1 mark for a valid counter-point and 1 mark for developing it [4]

items.stem: Mei is planning an answer to the question: “How far did the Cold War shape the US economy, 1945-68?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Mei could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: the Cold War economy was a major support for growth and shaped its regional pattern, but consumer demand was the main engine. Support: Defence spending stimulated industry and technology. Aerospace and electronics grew in the Sunbelt. Challenge: Consumer demand was the main engine of growth. Housing and the car industry drove the boom.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Nixon introduced a temporary freeze on wages and prices in 1971.” Is this accurate? Explain your answer using your own knowledge.
items.answer: Accurate. It was part of the New Economic Policy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a correct judgement; 1 mark for accurate supporting knowledge [2]

items.stem: Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: Inflation was below 3 per cent throughout the 1970s.
Poverty disappeared in the USA during the 1950s.
Nixon introduced a temporary freeze on wages and prices in 1971.
items.answer: Nixon introduced a temporary freeze on wages and prices in 1971.
items.markingKey: It was part of the New Economic Policy. The other statements are inaccurate. [1]

items.stem: Sofia is planning an answer to the question: “How effectively did US presidents deal with the economic problems of the 1970s?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Sofia could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: presidents were largely ineffective, though Carter's appointment of Volcker began the cure. Support: Nixon's controls briefly slowed inflation. Carter appointed Volcker, whose policies eventually ended high inflation. Challenge: Controls caused shortages and inflation returned. Ford's WIN campaign achieved little.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.answer: Accurate. It fell from 13.5 per cent in 1980 to about 3 per cent in 1983.

items.stem: How far did Reagan's economic policies benefit all Americans?
items.answer: For: Unemployment fell after 1983. Lower inflation helped savers and consumers. Tax cuts applied to all income groups. Against: Top earners gained most. Cuts in social programmes hurt the poor. Industrial workers lost jobs in the Rust Belt. Judgement: most Americans were better off by 1989 than in 1980, but the gains were very unequal.
